text: Figure 8.1: Composition assembled from several components using splitable elements The OEM provides the Composition A including a require port (left side) and a provide port (right side). Initially this Composition A does not contain any Atomic Software Components and will be persisted in one ARXML file, see listing G.5. Additionally , the OEM requires the integration of a predefined Atomic Software Com- ponent (SW-C X) by supplier X e.g. to include a brand-specific functionality . Also the Atomic Software Component (SW-C X) will be persisted in a dedicated ARXML file, see listing G.6. T o complete the functionality of the Composition A, the supplier Y has to develop and integrate the Atomic Software Component SW-C Y , see listing G.7. The splitting feature allows to adapt the implementation in an optimized way to the existing development process. The ARPackage SW-C Y is split e.g. in separate port definitions. They ensure the interaction with the Composition A and the Atomic Soft- ware Component (SW-C X), see listing G.8 and listing G.9. Another motivation for splitting could be to add further aspects to an element without changing the original artifact. In case the Internal Behavior is developed in two steps, a first step could define e.g. a rough calculation (Runnable 1) and a later step in the development process refines this calculation by a second calculation (Runnable 2), two splitable artifacts are useful (see listing G.10 and listing G.11). For the described collaboration scenarios it is important that the partial models devel- oped by different stakeholders can be merged - as far as possible - automatically into a common model based on clear rules. Remaining merge conflicts must be detected and reported. emplate
